source.title: Evaluation of Exertional Sweat Loss Estimates in Wearable Technology

paper.citation: Carrier B., Melvin A.C., Outwin J.R., Wasserman M.G., Audet A.P., Soldes K.C., et al. Evaluation of Exertional Sweat Loss Estimates in Wearable Technology. Sports Health: A Multidisciplinary Approach. 2026;18(3):507-520. doi:10.1177/19417381251388642.
paper.abstract: This paper addresses the following question: How accurately do the Samsung Galaxy Watch5 and Garmin Forerunner 945 estimate sweat loss during running compared with change in nude body mass? Participants: 111 physically active adults, age 40 ± 14 years, body mass 70.8 ± 14.7 kg, and VO₂max 46.8 ± 8.7 mL/kg/min. Sport and level: Recreationally active runners rather than a sport-team or elite-athlete sample. Design: Cross-sectional concurrent-validity study within a repeated testing protocol. Exposure or intervention: Up to three sweat-loss running trials per participant using fixed device/software versions.
paper.tldr: Across 293 completed running trials, the devices produced 291 paired estimates; criterion sweat loss averaged 658.57 mL and ranged from 80 to 3,300 mL. Samsung had MAE 151.05 mL, MAPE 25.38%, and CCC 0.90; Garmin had MAE 217.58 mL, MAPE 33.21%, and CCC 0.77. The tested smartwatch sweat-loss values should not be used as stand-alone prescriptions for individualized fluid replacement.
paper.methods: Design: Cross-sectional concurrent-validity study within a repeated testing protocol. Exposure or intervention: Up to three sweat-loss running trials per participant using fixed device/software versions. Comparator: Criterion sweat loss from pre/post nude body mass with fluid intake and urine output restricted around trials. Measurements and outcomes: Smartwatch-estimated sweat loss, mean absolute error, mean absolute percentage error, concordance and Pearson correlations, Deming regression, equivalence testing, and Bland–Altman agreement. Analysis: Overall and stratified validation by distance, environment, sex, body mass, and fitness; combined validity required MAPE 0.7, and supported equivalence.
paper.findings: Across 293 completed running trials, the devices produced 291 paired estimates; criterion sweat loss averaged 658.57 mL and ranged from 80 to 3,300 mL. Samsung had MAE 151.05 mL, MAPE 25.38%, and CCC 0.90; Garmin had MAE 217.58 mL, MAPE 33.21%, and CCC 0.77. Equivalence was not supported for either device, and Bland–Altman limits of agreement were −428.61 to 490.62 mL for Samsung and −464.01 to 726.73 mL for Garmin. No distance, environment, sex, body-mass, or fitness-level stratification met the authors' combined validity criteria. Distance, environment, and their interaction did not significantly change device error in MANOVA, but this null result does not establish equivalence across all environmental conditions.
paper.limitations: Proprietary algorithms are not public and may change with hardware or software updates, so these device/version-specific estimates can drift. Participants were not fully randomized to the variable-distance condition, and temperature and humidity were not included in the analysis. Wrist placement was standardized rather than randomized. Validation covered running to 20 km, criterion losses up to 3,300 mL, and body-mass losses up to about 2.7%; accuracy outside those conditions is unknown. The sample's mean age, body mass, fitness, activity, and running context differ from collegiate American-football athletes wearing protective equipment in hot practice environments. Acceptable CCC values reflect covariation, not individual-level agreement; the large percentage errors and limits of agreement are the decision-relevant validation results.
paper.practicalImplications: The tested smartwatch sweat-loss values should not be used as stand-alone prescriptions for individualized fluid replacement. When accuracy matters, staff should retain standardized pre/post body-mass procedures with recorded fluid intake and output. A watch estimate may be treated as a coarse exploratory trend only after local validation on the exact device, firmware, athlete population, activity, and environment—and even then should not override symptoms, clinical judgment, or established heat-safety procedures.

paper.rtp: For rehabilitation and return-to-sport decisions, the tested smartwatch sweat-loss values should not be used as stand-alone prescriptions for individualized fluid replacement. When accuracy matters, staff should retain standardized pre/post body-mass procedures with recorded fluid intake and output. A watch estimate may be treated as a coarse exploratory trend only after local validation on the exact device, firmware, athlete population, activity, and environment—and even then should not override symptoms, clinical judgment, or established heat-safety procedures. Use the paper as one input to interdisciplinary judgment, not as a standalone clearance criterion or reinjury prediction rule.
